newsitem.title: INDIA: India bank IPOs to get lukewarm response-analysts.
newsitem.headline: India bank IPOs to get lukewarm response-analysts.

text.p: India's lumbering state-run banks, which plan initial public offerings worth up to 20 billion rupees ($562 million) this fiscal year, will struggle to find buyers among shell-shocked investors, analysts said on Friday.
"It's going to be a bit of a fight," said Aditya Narain, banking analyst at UBS Securities.
Under financial sector reforms initiated in 1991, India's central bank instructed state-run banks to strengthen their capital base and get bad loans off the books.
Earlier this week, Dena Bank announced an October 28 date for the opening of its 1.8 billion rupee offering and Bank of Baroda said its 8.5 billion rupee issue would open December 5.
Large IPOs from Canara Bank, Corporation Bank and Bank of India are due to be launched by the end of the fiscal year ending March 31, 1997.

"We know we are coming into a very adverse market but if we succeed we may help in a modest way to revive the capital markets," Ramesh Mishra, chairman of Dena Bank, told a news conference on Thursday.
Those markets have taken a pounding in recent months, with Bombay's benchmark stock index falling 18 percent since India's budget announcement on July 22.
Analysts expect share prices to fall further on the back of a slowdown in industrial production and expected weak first-half results due to be announced in late October and November.
Analysts say Dena Bank's issue is overpriced at a price-to-earnings ratio (PER) of 8.52.

Investors looking for financial shares would rather pick up those of listed state-run banks Oriental Bank of Commerce and State Bank of India (SBI), which are available at more competitive PERs, said Prabhod Aggarwal, banking analyst at securities firm James Capel B&K.
In an attempt to lure retail investors, Bank of Baroda has said it will allow investors to pay the offer price of 85 rupees a share in three instalments.
Dena Bank's issue has not been underwritten and the bank plans to depend on employees and customers to fill up subscription.
"They will push the issue through employees and customers. The issue might scrape through but it will seriously affect the pricing of other issues that follow," Narain said.

Those other IPOs, scheduled for the 1997/98 fiscal year, include Punjab National Bank and three regional associates of SBI. Those IPOs are aimed at raising a further 15 billion rupees, said Girish Kumar, banking analyst at Merrill Lynch & Co in Singapore.
Narain said the IPOs were likely to keep SBI's share price in a tailspin. The shares have fallen 53 percent since July.
"I don't see SBI's share reviving until all of (the IPOs) are out of the way," he said.
But Kumar of Merrill Lynch said both banks and investors could benefit over the long term.

"If economic growth continues at five to six percent in the next six years banks will have a good opportunity to clean up their books and this will rub off positively on asset quality and be reflected in higher share prices," he said, adding that investors would favour stocks of the larger and more efficient banks.
Kumar said banking stocks accounted for only five percent of the country's total market capitalisation against 20-25 percent in countries like Thailand and Malaysia.
He said the forthcoming issues would double the weighting of banking stocks.
